paras: The lynching of Mack Taylor was the killing of a 14-year-old Black boy in Webster Parish, Louisiana, in June 1882 by three white men who seized him in Arkansas, brought him back, tied him to a tree and shot him. A coroner's jury named Edward McDonald, the father of a white boy Taylor was accused of beating, and two men who helped him. A Shreveport dispatch describing the remains as picked bare by vultures ran in papers across the country under headlines of revenge and butchery.

According to the Webster Tribune, about the first of the month Taylor got into a fight with some white boys and knocked down the son of Edward McDonald with a plow handle. The blow was described as so severe that the boy's life was for a time thought to be in danger, and Taylor ran away to Arkansas.

McDonald, assisted by J. J. Pickett and John Ammond, went into Arkansas, captured Taylor and brought him back to Webster Parish; the Tribune called it a kidnapping. In the woods the men tied him to a pine tree and shot him in the head, and the inquest found that McDonald had fired a charge of 12 buckshot. His body was left where he died, and when the remains were found nearly all the flesh had been picked from the bones.

Coroner Cheshire held an inquest on the 22nd, and the jury decided that Taylor had died by the hands of Edward McDonald, aided by Pickett and Ammond. The wire dispatches said that 'the assassins will be arrested', while the Emporia Weekly News printed that they had been arrested. No report of an arrest, indictment or trial appears in the coverage.

The first printed account came from the local Webster Tribune, reprinted by the Claiborne Guardian of Homer on July 5, which gave the inquest verdict and the names without comment. On July 10 a Shreveport special to the St. Louis Post-Dispatch, and a shorter National Associated Press version, carried the story nationally, reporting that the remains had just been found. Copy editors garbled the names, turning Taylor into 'McTaylor' and 'M. C. Taylor' and Pickett into 'Hickeland', 'Licket' and 'P. Net'.

Headlines framed the killing as a father's vengeance: the Washington Evening Star ran 'FEARFUL REVENGE OF A FATHER', the Savannah Morning News 'Terrible Vengeance in Louisiana', and the Omaha Daily Bee 'BLOODY REVENGE'. Other papers called it a crime, from the Memphis Daily Appeal's 'A Terrible Crime' to the Salt Lake Herald's 'Brutal Butchery' and the Sacramento Daily Record-Union's 'A Feast for the Vultures'. The St. Paul Daily Globe put the story under 'Another "Outrage."', setting the word in quotation marks. By July 18 the story had shrunk to one line in a Kentucky news column, which placed the killing 'at Shreveport'; no Black-press coverage survives for this year.

The wire dated the discovery to July 9 or 10, and one copy to a Tuesday, but the local paper had already reported an inquest held on the 22nd, which places the killing and the finding of the body in June.

reader.title: Lynching of Mack Taylor
bases: Three named white men pursued a Black boy accused of beating a white boy, took him from Arkansas back to Webster Parish, tied him to a tree and shot him (A1, A4, A23).

A coroner's jury found Taylor was shot by Edward McDonald aided by J. J. Pickett and John Ammond, private men who kidnapped him from Arkansas (A1); the wire called it revenge for his alleged beating of McDonald's son and named three men (A3, A4, A23).

The local Webster Tribune account with an inquest verdict (A1) and the separate Shreveport wire dispatches (A3, A4, A23) agree on the victim, the three men, the flight to Arkansas and the shooting at a tree.

accounts.label: Webster Tribune and coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Taylor hit McDonald's son with a plow handle and fled; the three men kidnapped him in Arkansas, tied him to a pine, shot him in the head and left him for dogs and vultures; the inquest named all three.

accounts.label: Shreveport wire (Post-Dispatch special)
accounts.gist: The remains were found tied to a tree in Webster Parish woods, flesh picked away by vultures; McDonald's father and two named men had pursued, captured and shot the boy, and 'the assassins will be arrested'.

framing.detail: Nearly every paper ran the Shreveport dispatch nearly verbatim, calling the killers 'assassins' and the act revenge.
Northern and western headlines called it 'Brutal Butchery', 'A Terrible Crime', 'Terrible Murder in Louisiana—A Feast for the Vultures', and, in St. Paul, 'Another "Outrage."'.
The Louisiana local account named the men and the inquest finding and described a kidnapping, without editorial comment.

versions.value: Inquest already held on 'the 22nd inst.' (June) per a July 5 Louisiana paper

conflicts.note: The local account, printed July 5 with an inquest verdict, is the better evidence that the killing and discovery came in June; the wire's 'this morning' and 'yesterday' are relative to a July 10 dispatch and cannot both be right.
The Dakotaian headline 'ASSASSINS ARRESTED' sits over text saying 'will be arrested' (A2); no report of an actual arrest was found.
The one-line Kentucky summary confused the dateline with the place.

record_check.dossier: July 10 is the wire dispatch date; the killing came in June 1882, before an inquest on the 22nd reported in a July 5 paper.
Edward McDonald, J. J. Pickett and John Ammond, named by the coroner's jury and the wire.
Three private men (the injured boy's father and two others), not a sworn posse; no officer took part.
Pursued and kidnapped from Arkansas while a fugitive (in pursuit).

record_check.dossier: Captured by the injured boy's father (Edward McDonald), not Taylor's father; an inquest named all three.
